workplace.title: The deadline moved
workplace.setting: Ivan tells his colleague Dana the client meeting is two days earlier.

lines.t: Dana, quick heads up. The client moved the meeting to Wednesday.
Wednesday? That's two days earlier. Where are we with the proposal?
About half done. I'd rather cut the scope than send something weak.
Agreed. Which sections actually matter to them?
That's what I asked them. They said pricing, timeline and the team.
So the market analysis can go. That saves you a day.
Can I run the new structure by you before I write it?
Send it over. I have the bandwidth this afternoon.
Thanks. I'll keep you posted if anything changes.
Do that. And let's not touch it after six, it's already been a long week.

workplace.title: Too much on my plate
workplace.setting: A manager asks someone to take on another project.

lines.t: Elena, could you take on the onboarding project as well?
I'd like to, but I have too much on my plate this month.
What's taking most of your time?
The two client reports and covering for Stefan while he's away.
Right. When does Stefan get back?
The fifteenth. After that I'd have the bandwidth.
Let's pencil it in for the sixteenth, then.
That works. Can we go over the scope before it starts?
Of course. I'll set up a short call for Friday.
Perfect. Then I can hit the ground running.

business.title: Getting buy-in
business.setting: Two managers discuss a restructure before presenting it.

lines.t: Before we take this to the board, we need buy-in from the regional heads.
All four of them? Two will push back hard.
Probably. What's their main objection?
Headcount. They think restructuring is a word for cutting jobs.
It isn't, and we should say that in plain language at the town hall.
Then we need numbers. How many roles actually change?
Eleven people get a new line manager. Nobody is made redundant.
Say exactly that. Vague answers are what start the rumours.
Agreed. I'll put it on one slide and take questions for as long as they last.
Good. And get sign-off from HR before Thursday.

business.title: The counteroffer
business.setting: A supplier responds to a client's much lower offer.

lines.t: We've reviewed your quote. Our counteroffer is 38% lower.
That's a big gap. Can I ask what's driving the number?
Procurement has a fixed budget for this category.
Understood. At that price I'd be taking teachers off profitable work.
So it's a no?
It's a different yes. Three locations instead of nine, at our rate.
A pilot, effectively.
Exactly. With an option to extend if the results hold.
I'll take that back to the team. It might get through faster, actually.
Take your time. The offer stands until the end of the quarter.

sales.title: It's too expensive
sales.setting: A salesperson meets a price objection on the fourth call.

lines.t: We like the programme, but honestly, it's too expensive.
Too expensive compared to what?
Compared to doing nothing, I suppose. We tried training two years ago.
And what happened?
People stopped attending after three weeks. We paid for the whole thing.
So the real question isn't price. It's whether it will happen this time.
That's fair.
Then let's start with one department, and tie the rest to attendance.
Meaning if attendance drops, we stop?
No penalty. If it works, we continue. Would that be easier to approve?
Considerably. Send it that way and I'll walk it through myself.

sales.title: Qualifying the lead
sales.setting: A first call with a company that downloaded a guide.

lines.t: Thanks for making time. You downloaded our assessment guide last week.
Yes, I was curious. We have people who struggle on calls in English.
How many people, roughly?
Maybe twenty in customer service.
And is there a budget for training this year?
There's a training budget, but I don't control it.
Who does?
The operations director. She signs off anything over five thousand.
Would it help if I prepared a short summary you could forward to her?
That would help a lot. One page, if possible.
One page it is. I'll send it today and follow up on Thursday.

marketing.title: Why the ad failed
marketing.setting: Reviewing a campaign that got clicks but no leads.

lines.t: Fifty thousand impressions and four leads. What went wrong?
The click-through rate was fine. The landing page lost them.
What's on it?
Our history, our team, three paragraphs about quality.
And the call to action?
At the bottom. It says 'Learn more', which asks for nothing.
So the ad promised a solution and the page talked about us.
Exactly. I'd rewrite it around one pain point and one action.
Do that, and let's A/B test two headlines before we spend more.
Agreed. Same budget, two weeks, then we compare conversion rates.

marketing.title: Planning the content calendar
marketing.setting: Two colleagues plan next month's posts.

lines.t: We need the content calendar for October by Friday.
How many posts a week are we doing now?
Three. Two useful, one behind the scenes.
The behind the scenes ones get the most engagement, by far.
Then let's make it two of those and one offer.
What about the lead magnet? It's been the same PDF since spring.
Good point. A fresh one would give us something to talk about.
I'll draft it. Something short, ten email templates maybe.
Perfect. That's evergreen content, we can use it all year.
I'll have a draft by Wednesday so you can review it.

customerservice.title: The angry caller
customerservice.setting: A customer has been transferred twice and is losing patience.

lines.t: This is the third time I've explained this. Nobody has called me back.
You've told this story three times already, and that's our fault, not yours.
Well. Thank you for saying that.
Let me take ownership of it now. Could you give me your order number?
It's WT four four nine one.
Thank you. I can see it. The delivery is four days late, with no update sent.
So when will it actually arrive?
Thursday is realistic. I could say Wednesday, but I'd rather be honest.
I appreciate that.
I'll send the tracking number now, and I'll call you myself if anything changes.
That's all I wanted from the start, really.

customerservice.title: A refund request
customerservice.setting: A customer wants money back outside the returns policy.

lines.t: I'd like a refund. The course wasn't what I expected.
I'm sorry to hear that. May I ask what was different?
I thought it was one to one. It's a group of eight.
I understand. Could I check when you enrolled?
About six weeks ago.
Our returns policy covers thirty days, so a full refund isn't possible.
That's disappointing.
It is. What I can do is move you to the one-to-one track and credit what you've used.
So I'd only pay the difference?
Exactly. Shall I check availability for next month?
Yes, please. That's a fair solution.

hr.title: The exit interview
hr.setting: An HR manager talks to someone who has handed in their notice.

lines.t: Thanks for doing this. There's nothing to lose by being direct.
All right. It wasn't the money, if that's the first question.
It was, actually. So what was it?
The shifts. They're published on Friday for the following Monday.
And that made life outside work impossible to plan.
I cancelled the same course three times. Eventually I stopped booking things.
Did you raise it with your line manager?
Twice. I was told it's how the department works.
That's useful, and I'm sorry it took your resignation for me to hear it.
Fix it for the others and I'll consider that a good outcome.

hr.title: Asking for a pay rise
hr.setting: An employee raises salary in a performance review.

lines.t: Before we finish, I'd like to talk about my salary.
Go ahead.
I've taken on the reporting and I'm training two new starters.
Both true. What figure did you have in mind?
Twelve per cent, which brings me in line with the market for this role.
That's above what I can approve alone. I'd need to build a case.
What would make that case stronger?
Numbers. How much time the new reporting saves the team each month.
I can put that together this week.
Do that, and I'll take it to the head of department in the next cycle.

finance.title: Profitable but broke
finance.setting: An owner and her accountant look at why cash is tight.

lines.t: We had our best year, and I nearly couldn't pay salaries in November.
That's not a profit problem. That's cash flow.
The profit margin held at nineteen per cent.
And accounts receivable is thirty-four thousand, most of it overdue.
Two clients treat sixty days as a suggestion.
Then ask for thirty per cent upfront on every new contract.
Won't that scare people off?
Some will push back. Almost nobody actually leaves.
And the ones already late?
Chase on day thirty-one, not day sixty-one. A short polite email.

finance.title: The quote was too low
finance.setting: Reviewing a project that came in under the break-even point.

lines.t: We made a three per cent margin. Our break-even point is twelve.
I know. The pages took three times longer than normal text.
Did we see a sample before quoting?
No. The client said the budget was tight, so I ran the numbers quickly.
And discounted fifteen per cent before knowing the scope.
Yes. They accepted the same day, which should have warned me.
It usually does. Let's make one rule from this.
No quote without a sample of the real material.
And no discount before the scope is clear.
Agreed. I'll put it in the template so nobody forgets.

accounting.title: Forty-eight euro
accounting.setting: A supervisor asks a bookkeeper not to write off a small difference.

lines.t: The bank reconciliation is out by forty-eight euro. Everything else matches.
What were you going to do with it?
Post an adjustment. It's below materiality and it's Friday.
Give it thirty minutes first. Where does the forty-eight come from?
A courier charge. It's in the purchase ledger and in office costs.
So it's a duplicate. Have you looked for others from that supplier?
Not yet. Give me a moment... there are eleven more across the year.
Which means costs are overstated and profit is understated.
One thousand three hundred and forty euro in total.
Small differences are rarely small. Write a note for the file.

accounting.title: Why December looks bad
accounting.setting: Explaining non-cash adjustments to a director.

lines.t: November showed nine thousand profit. December shows almost nothing.
Three things landed in December, and none of them are cash.
Go on.
The annual insurance was posted in full instead of as a prepayment.
So it should be spread over twelve months.
Yes. Second, a provision for the disputed invoice.
And the third?
Depreciation on the new equipment started. Seven hundred a month.
So the bank balance is actually fine.
Higher than November. Always ask what moved that isn't cash.

administration.title: Double-booked
administration.setting: Two meetings are scheduled in the same room at the same time.

lines.t: The big room is double-booked at eleven. Two teams, both confirmed.
Who booked first?
The finance review, three weeks ago.
Then they keep it. Can the other one move?
I can reschedule it to one o'clock or move it to the small room.
How many people?
Nine, so the small room would be tight.
Reschedule, then. Ask them, don't tell them.
I'll offer one and three and let them choose.
Perfect. And block out the room properly this time.

administration.title: Nine steps to five
administration.setting: An office coordinator proposes cutting an enrolment process.

lines.t: Enrolling one student takes nine steps and about twenty-five minutes.
With two hundred a month, that's a lot of hours.
Eighty-three. I asked one question about each step.
Which was?
Who reads this, and what happens if it doesn't exist?
And?
Two steps had no answer at all. The certificate template and the folder.
Nobody has opened those folders since 2023.
Exactly. And the spreadsheet and timetable can pull from one source.
Do it. Send me the new workflow on one page.

it.title: Roll back first
it.setting: A release breaks saved settings four minutes after going live.

lines.t: Nine emails in four minutes. People log in and their settings are empty.
Rolling back now. I'll look at the cause afterwards.
Don't you want to find the bug first?
Not while customers are affected. Restore service, then investigate.
How long will the roll back take?
About ten minutes. Tell people it's a known issue and we're on it.
Done. Any idea what caused it?
A migration renamed a column and the back end still asks for the old name.
The tests didn't catch that?
They used fresh accounts with no saved settings. That changes today.

it.title: The suspicious attachment
it.setting: Someone in accounts opened a file that shouldn't have been opened.

lines.t: I think I've done something bad. I opened an invoice attachment.
Is your computer still connected to the network?
Yes.
Unplug the cable now, and turn off the wifi. Don't shut it down.
Done. Some files have strange names now.
That's ransomware. The backups ran at two this morning, so we're fine.
I'm really sorry.
The email copied a real supplier exactly. You're not the first.
What happens now?
I restore from backup, and I tell everyone what to look for. No lecture.

legal.title: Clause 14
legal.setting: A client and legal counsel discuss a late delivery.

lines.t: They're six weeks late. I want to cancel and claim damages.
They'll argue force majeure. The factory flooded.
So we're stuck?
Not necessarily. Clause 14 requires written notice within forty-eight hours.
And they said nothing for eleven days.
That's the point that matters. The delay might be excusable, the silence isn't.
Do we go to court?
I'd settle out of court. Litigation costs more than the invoice.
What would a fair settlement look like?
A credit against the next order, and we amend the notice clause.

legal.title: Sign first, talk second
legal.setting: A founder learns why the NDA didn't protect them.

lines.t: They launched a copy of our pricing model. Can we sue?
When did you sign the non-disclosure agreement?
In May.
And when did you explain the model to them?
March. Two friendly meetings.
Then it sits outside the agreement. The NDA only covers what came after.
Isn't the model our intellectual property?
A business idea usually isn't. A patent or copyright would be.
That's an expensive lesson.
One sentence long. Sign first, talk second.

healthcare.title: Two minutes at the bedside
healthcare.setting: A junior doctor asks a patient why he has stopped eating.

lines.t: Good morning. I noticed you haven't eaten since yesterday.
I'm not very hungry.
Your tests are all normal, so I wondered if something else was wrong.
It's silly, really.
Tell me anyway. I have two minutes and nowhere else to be.
If I eat, I'll need the toilet. I can't reach it on my own.
And you didn't want to trouble the nurses.
They're busy. So I thought I'd manage until I go home.
Let me move your call bell closer, and I'll tell the ward.
That's all it takes? Then I'll have lunch.

healthcare.title: The waiting list
healthcare.setting: A manager shows a consultant why capacity is being lost.

lines.t: The waiting list is nine months. You asked for two more staff.
Because we can't see enough patients.
Eighteen per cent of appointments are no-shows.
That's higher than I thought.
And twelve per cent arrive without a referral, so they're turned away.
Almost a third of the capacity, before anyone is treated.
A text message two days before, and a check when booking.
And a short-notice list for slots that open up.
Exactly. No new staff, no new equipment.
I've been treating a process problem as a resource problem for three years.

hospitality.title: Room 402
hospitality.setting: A couple arrives at 9pm and the hotel is overbooked by one.

lines.t: Good evening. We have a reservation for two nights, the name is Ivanov.
Let me check... I'm very sorry. We're overbooked and there's no room tonight.
We booked six weeks ago.
You did, and this is our mistake, not a problem with your booking.
So what happens now?
I've held a room at our partner hotel, four minutes away, and we pay the taxi.
And tomorrow?
Room 402 here, sea view, at the rate you originally booked.
That's better than I expected, honestly.
I'd rather tell you straight than hide behind the word 'system'.

hospitality.title: A nut allergy on a full Saturday
hospitality.setting: A waiter takes an order on the busiest night of the year.

lines.t: Before we order, I should say I have a serious nut allergy.
Thank you for telling me. I'll write it in red and repeat it to the kitchen.
Even a small amount is a problem.
Understood. Are you happy for me to check each dish with the chef?
Please do.
The starters are fine. I'd avoid the dessert with the crumb topping.
Is there an alternative?
The sorbet, and I'll confirm the whole ticket with the pastry section.
You've done this before.
Every allergy gets read back twice. It takes eight seconds and it matters.

technical.title: Not the sensor
technical.setting: An engineer refuses to replace a part for the fifth time.

lines.t: Same fault again. Just swap the sensor and get the line running.
That's the fifth sensor this week. I'd like two hours instead.
Downtime costs nine hundred an hour.
And we've paid that four times already for a part that isn't broken.
You think the sensors are fine?
I think they're reporting a real problem accurately.
All right. What's your plan?
Shut down properly, lock out, and look at everything around the sensor.
Two hours. Then we do it your way or mine.
Fair. If I'm wrong, I'll fit the fifth sensor myself.

technical.title: Handover on the twelfth
technical.setting: A client engineer refuses to sign off with 63 items open.

lines.t: We're ready for handover on the twelfth as agreed.
The punch list still has sixty-three items.
All small. Sealant, paint, two door handles.
I know. And after handover, nobody is on site to fix them.
We'd come back.
Sixty-three becomes forty in a month and stays there for a year.
So what are you proposing?
Work the weekend, clear the list below ten, and hand over on the fifteenth.
Three days late.
In writing, agreed by the client, with the as-built drawings complete.

sport.title: Six weeks off
sport.setting: A physiotherapist explains an injury to a runner.

lines.t: How bad is it? I've got a race in October.
You've sprained the ankle. Six weeks, no running.
Six weeks? I haven't missed a session in two years.
I know. That's part of why it happened.
So I just sit still?
No. Swimming from week two, and upper body from tomorrow.
That's not really training.
It's training the parts you've ignored for years.
And October?
Possible, if you treat rest as part of the plan, not a break from it.

sport.title: Before the final
sport.setting: A coach talks to the team before a match everyone expects them to lose.

lines.t: They beat us four nil in November.
They did. Every newspaper has already picked them.
That's not helping.
It should. They have to win. We only have to play.
And if they score first?
Then we're where everyone expects us to be, and nothing has changed.
Home advantage is theirs too.
For ninety minutes it's eleven against eleven and a referee.
You really think we can do this.
I think underdogs play better without pressure. Go and enjoy it.

nutrition.title: The smaller plate
nutrition.setting: A doctor talks to a patient who has tried three diets.

lines.t: I've tried three diets in two years. None of them lasted.
What do you actually eat on a normal Tuesday?
Nothing terrible. Bread, chicken, rice, a takeaway on Friday.
That sounds fine. How much of it?
A full plate. It's always been a full plate.
Then it's portion size, not the food. Nothing needs to be banned.
So what do I change?
Use a smaller plate, and stop eating in front of the television.
That's it?
It's boring, and boring is what people can still do in March.

nutrition.title: Reading the label
nutrition.setting: A nutritionist shows a class how to read packaging.

lines.t: It says low-fat and high in protein. That's healthy, isn't it?
Guess the sugar content. One small pot.
Maybe six grams?
Twenty-one. More than a standard chocolate bar.
But the front says nothing about that.
The front is advertising. The back is information.
What should I actually look at?
Per hundred grams: sugar, saturated fat, salt. Three lines.
And the ingredients?
Listed by quantity. If sugar is in the first three, you know what you're buying.

lifestyle.title: The phone in the kitchen
lifestyle.setting: Two colleagues compare notes on screen time.

lines.t: My screen time said six hours forty a day. I checked it twice.
What did you delete?
Nothing. I moved my charger to the kitchen.
That's all?
The first three nights were strange. I reached for a phone that wasn't there.
And now?
Four hours, and the last hour of the day is completely different.
I tried that once. I use my phone as an alarm clock.
So buy an alarm clock. Mine cost seven euro.
That is annoyingly simple. All right, I'll try it this week.

lifestyle.title: Saying no in November
lifestyle.setting: A brother and sister talk about too many commitments.

lines.t: Two committees, a weekend course, and the neighbour's renovation.
Do you enjoy any of them?
I attend all of them. That's not the same thing.
Write down why you said yes to each one.
That feels uncomfortable.
Do it anyway. I'll wait.
Seven of eleven say the same thing. It felt rude to refuse.
So cancel three tonight and see what actually happens.
And if people are offended?
Then you'll know. My guess is nobody will be, and that will annoy you.
